query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing minor aluminum adds to CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys promotes the formation of a slow-growing, coherent Al2O3 scale that remains adherent during prolonged exposure above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres, thereby mitigating the formation of unstable, spalling surface oxides seen in alloys without such aluminum.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloys in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state with a baseline composition lacking significant aluminum additions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, minor Al addition into the alloy composition, then compare these modified alloys against baseline (Al-lean) samples.
generation.conditions: Exposure at temperatures above 900 °C under oxidative or corrosive atmospheres with controlled duration (e.g., isothermal hold for several hours).
generation.structural_mediator: A coherently bonded, slow-growing Al2O3 layer that forms on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum preferentially oxidizes to form a stable, adherent Al2O3 scale. Its lower ionic diffusivity and growth kinetics as compared to chromium oxide facilitate the development of a protective, crack-resistant barrier, reducing deleterious oxide spallation. In contrast, the baseline alloys form less coherent oxides that crack and spall due to higher diffusion rates and volatile oxide species.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with the minor Al addition will exhibit a continuous and coherent Al2O3 scale, leading to reduced oxide cracking/spallation and improved high-temperature oxidation/corrosion resistance compared to the baseline alloys.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys without the deliberate minor Al addition, which are prone to developing unstable, spalling oxide scales under high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for alloys in single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution states undergoing oxidation at temperatures above 900 °C; results may vary outside this temperature range or under different atmospheric chemistries.
generation.uncertainty: The exact aluminum content needed for optimal oxide coherence and the long-term cyclic oxidation behavior remain to be quantified, and the effect might be modulated by the specific identity of the X element in the alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples: one set with a minor, controlled Al addition and one baseline set without Al addition. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation tests at >900 °C in a controlled oxidative/corrosive environment for a predetermined duration. Periodically analyze the surface using SEM, TEM, and EDS to assess oxide scale morphology, continuity, and compositional uniformity. Additionally, perform spallation and adhesion tests along with weight gain measurements to quantify protective behavior.
measurements: Composition and elemental distribution of the oxides (EDS/XPS analysis)
Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (cross-sectional analysis)
Weight change measurements to monitor oxidation kinetics
Adhesion/spallation resistance tests (e.g., scratch or pull-off testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloys do not form a significantly more coherent, slower-growing, and adherent Al2O3 scale—as evidenced by similar oxide morphology, spallation behavior, and oxidation kinetics compared to the baseline alloys—the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The oxidation behaviour of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA provides valuable insights into its suitability for high-temperature applications. This oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi HEA plays a critical role in determining its mechanical, thermal, and corrosion resistance properties in elevated temperature environments. The observed non-protective oxide formation, particularly the depletion of Mn in the bulk alloy, can have significant implications for this particular alloy’s mechanical properties. Mn is known to contribute to solid solution strengthening and can enhance the mechanical strength and ductility of alloys. Therefore, the formation of non-protective oxides and the depletion of Mn may negatively affect the mechanical performance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA at high temperatures.

One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. The high rate of heating and cooling and high oxygen concentration during spraying led to oxidation development prior to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution. Depleted Al layers of BCC transferred to the FCC phase. Enhanced properties are one of the key motivations for research on high entropy alloys (HEA) and compositionally complex alloys (CCA) []. Miracle and Senkov [] stated that “HEAs have been tightly associated with finding single-phase solid solutions by controlling configurational entropy”. Furthermore, and in line with a proposal by Miracle and Senkov [], we refer to multi-principal element alloys forming multiphase microstructures as complex concentrated alloys (CCAs). Contrary to the conventional alloys, HEAs are defined to contain five to 13 major constituting elements where the concentration of each element ranges from 5 to 35 at.% []. According to Zhang et al., the formation of HEAs is predicted for materials exhibiting 12 J K−1∙mol−1 (≈ 1.44∙R) ≤ configurational entropies ≤ 17.5 J∙K−1 mol−1 (≈ 2.10 R), −10 kJ∙mol−1 ≤ enthalpies of mixing ≤ 5 kJ∙mol−1 and atomic size differences ≤ 5% [], with R as the gas constant (≈ 8.3144 J K−1∙mol−1). However, over time, these guidelines were revealed not to be entirely successful at predicting the formation of single-phase solid solutions [,,,,].

AbstractHigh-entropy alloys could provide a solution for corrosion resistance due to their impressive properties. Solid-state processing of high purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni and Mo metallic powders and consolidation resulted in a bulk material that was further machined into electro spark deposition electrodes. After the stainless steel substrate surface preparation, thin successive layers of the high-entropy alloy were deposited and Pull-Off testing was performed on the newly obtained coating, for a better understanding of the adhesion efficiency of this technique. Good adhesion of the coating to the substrate was proved by the test and no cracks or exfoliations were present. Corrosion resistance testing was performed in a liquid solution of 3.5 wt.% NaCl for 6 h at room temperature and the results obtained validated our hypothesis that CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloys could provide corrosion resistance when coating a stainless steel substrate.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical alloying, coatings, adhesion

DS2205 and AlCoCrFeNi2.1 showed stable potential, which gradually increased towards a more noble value and lower fluctuations after ~1 h of exposure in the molten chloride salt at 450 °C. At 650 °C, both the alloys showed relatively poor stability for the first 30 min, suggesting that an increase in temperature might have resulted in the unstable growth of surface oxide initially, before reaching steady state. Figure 3b shows the potentiodynamic polarization curves for the two alloys after stable OCP at the temperatures of 450 °C and 650 °C. The corrosion current density (Icorr) for the two alloys was determined from Tafel analysis and is summarized in Table 3. The Icorr value increased with an increase in temperature for both alloys, indicating the high dissolution rate and relatively poor protective nature of their surface passivation layer. AlCoCrFeNi2.1 showed lower Icorr at 650 °C compared to DS2205, demonstrating its excellent corrosion resistance at the higher temperature.

reading.lever: Introduce and compare minor Al additions within CrFeCoNiX alloys to promote a slow‐growing, coherent Al2O3 scale.
reading.why: Prior evidence indicates Al addition forms protective Al2O3 at high temperatures, addressing oxide spallation issues in related systems.
